strap: A daily dispatch from the world you are entering

lead.title: Tech billionaires gained USD 845 billion in nine months while every other kind of fortune lost USD 62 billion, Bloomberg's index shows
lead.standfirst: The record divergence means the households a private service professional is most likely to be hired by are increasingly those of the technology founder.
lead.body:
The world's technology billionaires added a combined USD 845 billion to their fortunes in the first nine months of 2026, through 30 September, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. It is a record for the period. Over the same stretch, billionaires whose wealth comes from other industries collectively lost USD 62 billion, as reported by Quartz on 5 October.

The roughly 100 technology fortunes on the index now total USD 4.6 trillion, or 36 per cent of the index's combined wealth. The same week, Bloomberg reported that the artificial intelligence boom had lifted Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg into the top ten of its ranking, a sign of how quickly the head of the list is being redrawn by a single theme.

The concentration matters for anyone who serves wealthy families. Technology wealth tends to be younger, more liquid and more exposed to a single sector than the industrial, retail or property fortunes it is overtaking. It often arrives with households that are being built from scratch: first estates, first aircraft, first full-time staff, and a founder who has never employed a house manager.

It also tends to bring a different set of expectations, from data discipline and digital privacy to a preference for systems and clear reporting over informal arrangements. Families whose fortunes fell, by contrast, are more likely to be reviewing costs, which tends to show up first in hiring pauses and renegotiated vendor contracts.
lead.why: Where the wealth is growing is where new households are being formed, and the professional who understands a founder's world, its tools and its exposure to one sector, is the one who is hired to build it.
lead.src: Quartz, citing the Bloomberg Billionaires Index

articles.title: Fine wine edges up 2.1 per cent in nine months, led by Italy and Champagne, while Bordeaux stays flat
articles.body:
The Liv-ex 100, the benchmark of about 20 of the most traded fine wines, rose 2.1 per cent from January to September 2026 and 4.4 per cent over twelve months. The broader Liv-ex 1000 gained 1.3 per cent for the year to date and 2.2 per cent over twelve months, according to an analysis published by WineNews on 6 October.

Italy was the standout. The Italy 100 index rose 3.5 per cent year to date and 4.9 per cent over twelve months, the best of any regional index over the past year, and Italian labels hold four of the top ten places in the Liv-ex 100. Champagne 50 gained 4.1 per cent this year, Burgundy 150 rose 1.7 per cent and Rhône 100 rose 0.5 per cent. Bordeaux 500 fell 0.2 per cent and is the only index still negative for the year.

The best individual performers were Bruno Giacosa Barolo Falletto Vigna Le Rocche Riserva 2016, up 31.7 per cent, Giacomo Conterno Barolo Monfortino Riserva 2019, up 19.4 per cent, Soldera Case Basse 2020, up 18.7 per cent, and Antinori Solaia 2021, up 14.1 per cent. The analysis describes the wider wine market as still in a slump, which makes the gains a bright spot concentrated in a small niche of prestige bottles.

For a cellar, the picture is one of rotation rather than a rising tide. Collectors who built their holdings around Bordeaux are seeing little movement, while demand has moved towards the Langhe, Tuscany and grower Champagne.
articles.why: A house manager who looks after a cellar is expected to speak about what is moving and why, and to advise on what to drink, hold or insure, not only on where it is stored.

articles.title: Large-cabin jet sales fell about 25 per cent in the third quarter, yet six months of supply keeps the segment the tightest in the market
articles.body:
Sales of pre-owned large-cabin business jets fell roughly 25 per cent year on year in the third quarter of 2026, and the segment accounted for more than two thirds of the quarter's overall shortfall, according to GlobalAir.com's BrokerBeat report with data to 1 October. Sales for the twelve months to September were still 11 per cent ahead of the prior year, and September itself recovered to roughly the level of September 2025.

Supply has not eased. There were 178 active large-cabin listings, the most of any jet class, representing 6.0 months of supply, the shortest of any turbine segment. The median time on the market was 77 days, the fastest among jets. Large-cabin aircraft made up 37 per cent of the 107 Aircraft Wanted requests sent through BrokerNet in the quarter, the largest share of any class.

Dealers describe a market of selective buyers. One said demand for premium late-model aircraft remains strong, with some receiving offers above asking price. Another expects less of a year-end rush than last year, citing labour shortages, parts delays and limited availability of pre-purchase inspection slots. The October to December 2025 period was the strongest in two years of data, so this quarter faces a hard comparison. IADA-accredited dealers closed 746 deals in the first half, up 21 per cent.

On the delivery side, dealers expect new aircraft from manufacturers to ease supply, with some softening likely in early 2027.
articles.why: A family that owns or charters a large-cabin aircraft depends on its coordinator to understand when an aircraft can be inspected, repositioned or replaced, and a tight maintenance calendar is now part of that planning.

articles.title: UBS counts nearly one million new dollar millionaires as personal wealth grows by more than 10 per cent
articles.body:
The UBS Global Wealth Report 2026, the seventeenth edition, finds that personal wealth rose by more than 10 per cent, its fastest pace in several years. The number of US dollar millionaires grew again, adding nearly one million people worldwide, or more than 2,600 a day.

The report covers 56 markets that UBS says account for more than 92 per cent of the world's wealth, and it examines how the global wealth pyramid is shifting as faster-growing tiers reshape the picture of where affluence is emerging. The firm frames the analysis around how wealth is created, as well as how it is distributed across regions.

For the households at the very top, the relevant point is not the headcount of millionaires but the pace at which new wealth is being created and where. New fortunes mean new houses, new offices and new demand for people who can run them, and they tend to appear in markets where the private service profession is still young and agencies are few.
articles.why: The report is a map of where demand for private staff will come from next, and it rewards candidates who can read wealth data the way their employers do.

briefs.t: Three new yachts from 40 to 80 metres reach the water in a month
briefs.b: Custom Line launched its 40-metre Saetta 128 at Ancona on 8 October, while CRN delivered the 70-metre Cerulean on 16 September and ISA Yachts launched the 80-metre Belita on 15 September. Gulf Craft launched the 30-metre Nomad 101 Charisma on 12 October.
Embraer delivered the first Praetor 600E to Flexjet, the fleet launch customer, on 2 October. Flexjet is also due to receive its first Praetor 500E in the fourth quarter of 2026.

briefs.t: Autoland reaches more private cabins, and Northolt gains an FBO
briefs.b: Pilatus received EASA and FAA approval for Safety Autoland on the PC-12 PRO on 8 October, and Epic won FAA certification for Garmin Autoland on the E1000 AX on 12 October. Gama Aviation began FBO operations at RAF Northolt in West London on 2 October.
